explanation.heading: ### Keep allocation, identity and frame state separate
explanation.paragraph: The ignored native test in `objects/gpu_tests.rs` opens a headless device, moves one object row and verifies that its neighbour remains unchanged. Scaling must update that row's ambient radius while translation preserves it. The widget row must remain after all object rows and be reminted when another upload arrives. The test is ignored by default because it requires a native adapter; compiling it or reporting an ignored count is not evidence that these GPU-backed operations ran.

explanation.heading: ### Pass order and visibility
explanation.paragraph: `objects/ink.rs` builds the object binding used by ink shaders: object and translation buffers, both depth sample variants, both primitive-ID variants, projected triangles and tile lists. Rebinding must follow attachment or buffer replacement because the bind group holds resource handles. Picking builds the same contract over its own cropped depth/ID targets; borrowing the main image attachments would test visibility in the wrong pixel coordinates.

explanation.heading: ### Keep allocation, identity and frame state separate
explanation.paragraph: `objects/lane.rs` adapts the object table to the common `Lane` lifecycle. Reset delegates to logical row reset, release delegates to allocation release with device/layout access, and byte reporting includes its buffers with zero texture bytes. This small adapter is how the renderer can manage object rows alongside drawing lanes without duplicating their lifetime rules in the host.

explanation.heading: ### Ownership and allocation
explanation.paragraph: `InstanceTable::append` replaces the empty placeholder on the first upload. A widget row must remain last, so appending scene objects first removes that row and rebuilds the retained prefix. The table retains CPU rows because editing one field must preserve every other field. `write_at` uploads only the changed row; chunked writes keep individual transfers bounded. A geometry revision lets downstream caches distinguish a real geometry or visibility change from unchanged state.

explanation.heading: ### Presentation and pacing
explanation.paragraph: `FramePacing` prevents old camera frames accumulating behind a busy queue. `ready` records that a redraw is waiting, then rechecks completion to avoid losing a wakeup between those two operations. `submitted` installs a queue-completion callback; that callback clears the pending flag and requests a redraw only if one was waiting. The flags are shared through `Arc` because completion outlives the submitting call. Their acquire/release operations make the completion and waiter state visible across callbacks.

explanation.heading: ### Pass order and visibility
explanation.paragraph: `Pass` extends the lane lifecycle with hooks around these stages. `PASSES` registers instancing, clipping, ambient occlusion and surface outlines. During a mutable hook, `each_pass` temporarily replaces that pass with `Nothing`; the hook can then borrow the rest of `Gpu` without two mutable references to the same object. The original pass is restored afterwards. A later pass registers once rather than inserting calls throughout the frame loop.

explanation.heading: ### Keep allocation, identity and frame state separate
explanation.paragraph: `patch.rs` describes editable allocation in units of each lane, not one interchangeable row count. `Counts` stores vertex, face-index, printed-index, text-index, source-face, stroke, marker and registered-lane counts; `Span` pairs start offsets with those counts. Capacity fitting compares every lane. Byte accounting includes the associated CPU mirrors and source-ID storage, so its per-lane stride is not necessarily the packed GPU vertex stride. These contracts let the application decide whether a replacement fits an existing allocation without teaching the renderer about editing commands.

explanation.heading: ### Pass order and visibility
explanation.paragraph: `Picker` owns request, draw, copy, map and poll state. It clamps a cursor window to the framebuffer, adds a three-pixel visibility halo and uses a 256-byte-aligned readback row stride. A generation counter invalidates answers from cancelled requests. Source-point queries clear IDs on their first page and preserve them on later pages while reusing depth. Asynchronous map completion is published through an atomic flag; polling distinguishes no completed answer from a completed miss. Application input can consume that result without blocking the render loop for every pointer event.

explanation.heading: ### Generate planes and arrows from compact rows
explanation.paragraph: `PlaneLane` registers construction, row counting and merging in the same lane registry as other primitives. A plane occupies 48 bytes, checked on the Rust side, and one instanced draw generates 22 grid lines plus three arrows. The global plane size is stored as atomic f64 bits and copied to frame uniforms, so changing it changes the next drawing without rebuilding the frame rows. Buffer growth requires rebinding group three. Color and object-ID pipelines share the geometry, keeping a picked plane aligned with its visible drawing.

explanation.heading: ### Presentation and pacing
explanation.paragraph: `present.rs` writes shared uniforms, prepares the widget and text, and acquires a surface texture. Success and suboptimal acquisition proceed; any other acquisition result reconfigures the surface and skips that attempt. A successfully acquired frame is encoded, submitted and presented. Optional passes can compile further pipelines after presentation. Pending pipeline work or a visibility report may require a later redraw even when the user has stopped moving the mouse.

explanation.heading: ### Pass order and visibility
explanation.paragraph: `render.rs` first prepares registered passes, builds triangle visibility lists and projects cloud points. The face stage draws background, section caps, solid faces and cloud resolve while writing depth. Ambient occlusion and outline masks consume that result. The ink stage then draws borders, curves, registered lanes, markers and text. Selected mesh edges appear below the selection outline; selected curves appear above it. The widget uses its own depth so it remains usable over the scene.

explanation.heading: ### Strokes, dashes and reveal
explanation.paragraph: `SegRows` separates surface-edge pipes, editable ribbons and streamed sheet rows, with parallel tables for source IDs, chain ranges, dash lengths, cumulative offsets and trims. Upload expands a 40-byte segment into a 72-byte `StrokeSegment` carrying previous/next neighbours and visibility slack. A special neighbour code marks an end covered by an arrowhead; the sign bit of the sag field marks silhouette-only ink, including negative zero. Sheet chunks must continue the resident source interval in order. Keeping source intervals separate from GPU row offsets lets picking recover the original entity after chunked uploads.

explanation.heading: ### Keep allocation, identity and frame state separate
explanation.paragraph: `Slots` lets many placed objects draw one definition without duplicating its geometry. Each eight-byte instance entry carries an object row and triangle-ID base. Slot zero contains `OWN_ROW`, meaning ordinary draws keep the row already stored on each primitive. Definition draws use ranges of later slots; their vertex-buffer layout advances once per instance. Updating slots changes placement identity without rewriting vertices. Clearing can either keep capacity or release it, while restoring the mandatory slot-zero entry.

explanation.heading: ### Render resident cloud points
explanation.paragraph: `gpu/splat.rs` turns selected ranges into bounded draw records. A record carries the combined camera/object matrix, point and normal offsets, radius information, tint, owner row and selected point. Its 160-byte Rust layout matches the shader's 40-word stride. Cumulative point counts let `splat.wgsl` locate a record by binary search when a single draw spans several runs. Six generated vertices form each point's quad; the shader computes its actual coverage and depth.

explanation.heading: ### Identify the adapter behind a cloud image
explanation.paragraph: The cloud rendering witness requires positive viewport dimensions, density one or two, one or four samples and a finite nonnegative EDL setting. It verifies the CPU DX12 Microsoft Basic Render Driver before rendering an isolated cloud. The source is decoded and uploaded through the scene path; the fixture then checks its expected matrix, cloud and splat counts. Its result retains adapter identity, actual parameters, uploaded CPU bytes and shader source. Such a result is evidence for that software adapter and fixture, not physical GPU or phone acceptance.

explanation.heading: ### Inspect LOD selection separately from rendering
explanation.paragraph: The cloud LOD witness prepares production cloud rows, cloud metadata and bounds on the CPU, then invokes the actual `LodWalk::select` with a fixed eye and viewport plus explicit projection, placement and pixel threshold. It rejects a resident prefix larger than the source and reports each selected range's first point, count, spacing and tile. These ranges explain which resident points the selector chose. Its metadata explicitly excludes GPU acceptance: correct ranges cannot establish shader output, depth, EDL or the appearance of the rendered points.

explanation.heading: ### Reconstruct ambient shading from visible geometry
explanation.paragraph: `Ssao` owns the reduced-resolution depth, radius, normal, filtered-occlusion and history images. Its cached key combines frame uniforms with geometry revision: an unchanged view and scene can reuse the result. Camera changes can reuse reprojected history only while the geometry revision agrees; changed geometry invalidates that assumption. Bindings are rebuilt when depth, primitive IDs, geometry buffers or the slot table change. Image dimensions and device scale also determine whether existing resources fit. The pass runs after faces, because it needs their actual depth and primitive identity.

explanation.heading: ### Reconstruct ambient shading from visible geometry
explanation.paragraph: `ssao/pipelines.rs` constructs the pipeline family for preparing depth, reducing it, finding occupied regions, estimating occlusion, filtering, storing history, upsampling and compositing. Layouts distinguish depth, integer identity/radius, sampled floating-point images and storage buffers. The target sample count controls multisampled scene bindings, while reduced working images remain single-sampled. Treat this as one resource contract: selecting a shader entry point with the wrong texture sample type is a validation failure, not a visual-quality setting.

explanation.heading: ### Choose an assertion that detects the rendering defect
explanation.paragraph: The ambient-occlusion regression renders contact geometry with the effect off and on at one and four samples in perspective and orthographic views. It requires contact darkening, rejects a halo on distant exposed ground and compares the first shaded frame with the settled frame. Resource checks account for the effect's owned allocations. The test is ignored until a native adapter is explicitly supplied, so normal unit-test success does not establish its image result.

explanation.heading: ### Shade and outline the resulting surface coverage
explanation.paragraph: `surface_outline.rs` renders coverage masks, resolves multisampled coverage when needed, and builds coarse and dilated masks to skip empty regions. `face_coverage.wgsl` produces coverage; `surface_outline.wgsl` composites the border using a bounded offset table. Selection outlines and ordinary borders can then use the appropriate masks without confusing object IDs with coverage values.

explanation.heading: ### Choose an assertion that detects the rendering defect
explanation.paragraph: The outline regression compares selected and unselected CAD strokes over curved silhouettes at multiple views, sample counts and device ratios. Pixels that were nearly black must remain black when yellow selected edges are drawn, and total silhouette coverage must remain nontrivial. This catches edges painting over the border rather than only checking that both passes submitted. These native GPU tests require explicit execution beyond the default ignored set.

explanation.heading: ### Keep allocation, identity and frame state separate
explanation.paragraph: `Targets` owns depth, optional multisampled color and per-sample triangle-ID attachments for one size and sample count. Triangle IDs occupy two integer 16-bit channels. Shaders bind both single-sample and multisample views, so the unused variant receives a one-by-one placeholder with the correct sample type. Keeping those placeholders owned with the targets prevents dangling resource assumptions. A size or sample-count change requires matching targets and pipelines; changing only a texture cannot change the pipeline attachment contract.

explanation.heading: ### Prepare GPU data only when its inputs change
explanation.paragraph: `TextLane::prepare` keys work by document revision, font revision and relevant camera/canvas facts. If every label is fixed on screen, the key omits camera motion while retaining canvas dimensions. Otherwise projection changes require preparation. A matching key increments the skipped-preparation counter and retains the buffers.

explanation.heading: ### Prepare GPU data only when its inputs change
explanation.paragraph: Sheet lettering is different again: `text_outline.rs` draws existing arena geometry as unlit fills with color and identity pipelines, using `text_outline.wgsl`. It does not reshape those outlines as label strings. `glyphs.rs` and `glyph.wgsl` draw the renderer's geometry glyph lane, which also differs from the glyphon atlas used for ordinary labels.

explanation.heading: ### Prepare GPU data only when its inputs change
explanation.paragraph: `text_plane.rs` caches a texture for each world-plane label, keyed by the inputs needed to rasterize it, and draws textured geometry in the world. Dropping a cached plane destroys its texture. `text_plane.wgsl` supplies that color/identity path. `text_plate.rs` builds clipped background rectangles, places depth-tested rectangles before overlays, and retains color and ID pipelines. Its `text_plate.wgsl` shader therefore supports selectable plates as well as their visible backgrounds.

explanation.heading: ### Text resources
explanation.paragraph: `Plates::prepare` creates six vertices per label background, placing depth-tested rectangles before overlays. It preserves the original rectangle centre, half-size and corner radius before clipping the emitted quad to its screen box. That distinction prevents clipping from rounding a newly cut edge as though it were the original plate boundary. Each vertex carries optional object identity and selection; the physical vertex count separates the two depth policies within one buffer.

explanation.heading: ### Keep allocation, identity and frame state separate
explanation.paragraph: `PassTimer` is optional instrumentation, available only when the device supports both timestamp queries and timestamps inside encoders. It writes at most 32 marks, resolves them to a GPU buffer, copies to a readable buffer and converts adjacent tick differences using the queue timestamp period. Collection waits for GPU completion and unmaps the readback before reuse. These measured GPU spans are different from CPU command-encoding time; the blocking collection belongs to an explicit measurement run, not an assumed free operation in ordinary animation.

explanation.heading: ### Project once, then restrict each visibility query
explanation.paragraph: `project_triangles.wgsl` transforms triangles into screen-space records described by `projected_triangle.wgsl`. Each record carries clipped coverage, edge equations, bounds and depth information. `triangle_tiles.rs` manages those buffers and binds the current geometry, object transforms and slot table. If an allocation moves, it rebuilds the binding that holds the old handle.

explanation.heading: ### Upload and lifetime
explanation.paragraph: `prepare` frees textures retired by the previous frame, uploads the current texture deltas, and tessellates shapes into clipped triangles. The returned texture-free list is saved for the next frame. This delay keeps a texture alive while the current frame still references it. Vertex and index buffers are updated before the draw pass uses them; callback command buffers are submitted together with the upload encoder.

explanation.heading: ### Keep allocation, identity and frame state separate
explanation.paragraph: `Upload` owns the CPU rows waiting for transfer. Merging an upload moves each typed table, shifts mesh vertex indices by the destination vertex base and rebases valid face-source IDs; the all-ones missing-ID sentinel stays unchanged. Registered lanes merge through `REGISTRY`, so a new primitive family does not require changes throughout the upload loop. `drop_uploaded` replaces vectors with empty vectors and clears lane rows after transfer, freeing their capacity instead of retaining a second full CPU copy.

explanation.heading: ### Keep allocation, identity and frame state separate
explanation.paragraph: `Upload::pad` reserves hidden spare rows for a growing editable preview. It adds roughly half the requested counts, rounds index allocations to whole triangles and directs spare primitives to a sink row. Missing face and edge IDs use their explicit sentinels. The returned count difference records the actual allocation, including rounding. Spare allocation is not visible geometry: later edits can fill it without moving every following object, while the sink keeps unused rows from drawing.

explanation.heading: ### Generate planes and arrows from compact rows
explanation.paragraph: `VectorRow` is a checked 64-byte GPU record containing endpoints, pen, object identity, color, head settings and endpoint trims. The head bits independently select start, end and head-only drawing. `VectorLane` owns the row buffer and matching color/ID pipelines, while its registry entry provides creation, row counting, merge and stride. The draw generates eighteen vertices per row; it does not upload a separately tessellated arrowhead mesh.

explanation.heading: ### Keep allocation, identity and frame state separate
explanation.paragraph: `View` stores rendering choices separately from GPU allocation. Startup reads native environment variables or browser query values, clamps pen softness and opacity, and distinguishes line, mesh-edge, point and outline controls. Enabling Arctic shading also enables outlines. A coarse primary pointer selects solid default faces; the desktop default is 0.95 opacity. Browser device scale is capped at two unless an explicit valid cap is supplied, with reduced mode capped at one. A narrow viewport alone does not prove that the browser reports a touch-first device.

explanation.heading: ### Keep the manipulation widget independent of scene depth
explanation.paragraph: `Widget` renders that mesh into a small tile with its own depth, then composites the tile over the scene. Placement and active-handle state feed a 96-byte uniform containing the matrix, screen rectangle and settings. Off-screen or absent placement disables drawing. Clearing drops tile textures and active state; a changed canvas format rebuilds the composite pipeline. Separate depth keeps scene surfaces from hiding a handle needed to manipulate the selected object.

explanation.heading: ### Keep the manipulation widget independent of scene depth
explanation.paragraph: `widget_mesh.rs` constructs the reusable manipulation mesh from three lathed arrows, three quarter-ring tubes, three scale balls and a centre hub. Vertices carry position in CSS-sized widget coordinates, packed color and one of ten handle IDs. Shared arm, ball and hub constants come from the geometric model, keeping the displayed shape consistent with hit testing. This mesh is uploaded once; hovering a handle changes a uniform rather than regenerating vertices.

explanation.heading: ## Prerequisites and ownership
explanation.paragraph: `app/mod.rs` exposes application modules, beginning with the event-loop launcher. `engine/mod.rs` groups GPU, pipeline, timing and diagnostic ownership. `engine/gpu/mod.rs` exposes GPU resource and rendering modules, beginning with device setup. These files are namespace boundaries, not alternate event loops. The partial assembly retains the declarations it can satisfy; later subjects add module declarations and re-exports under the checked registration rule. Their implementations stay in the corresponding files throughout the sequence.

explanation.heading: ### Measure interaction and resting quality separately
explanation.paragraph: The performance controller distinguishes wheel bursts and drag frames from resting frames. It uses a recent median and hysteresis before changing interaction tiers, then restores resting quality. Timing an isolated CPU submission is not the same as waiting for GPU completion. Record the actual adapter, whether the run used software rendering, and whether timing includes startup, compilation or refinement.

explanation.heading: ### Describe bindings before supplying resources
explanation.paragraph: `pipelines/bindings.rs` builds individual layout entries. A buffer entry declares its shader stages and uniform or storage access, with no dynamic offset and no declared minimum size. A texture entry declares a two-dimensional view, sample type and whether it is multisampled. These declarations do not allocate resources. A depth texture and an unsigned integer identity texture can have the same dimensions while requiring different binding types.

explanation.heading: ### Compile a shared description on first use
explanation.paragraph: `pipelines/core.rs::Lazy<T>` owns an `Rc<LazyCell<T, ...>>`. `Rc` lets several owners share one value on the current thread. `LazyCell` calls its stored `FnOnce` constructor only when dereferenced; `FnOnce` permits consuming the captured pipeline description. Cloning the wrapper shares that cell instead of recompiling. Equality and hashing compare the shared allocation's identity, so two references to one lazy shader are the same key even before compilation.

explanation.heading: ### Device, uploads and frames
explanation.paragraph: `pipelines/geometry.rs` delegates the arena vertex layout to `GpuVertex`, keeping pipeline inputs synchronized with the packed storage format. Its ignored native test renders an empty frame, uploads a solid and alternates four- and one-sample targets. Compilation counts must grow on first use but stay unchanged when returning to an already compiled target; it also asks the cache to compile unused variants. This is an explicit adapter-dependent test of lazy pipeline ownership, not a result supplied by a documentation build.

explanation.heading: ### Describe bindings before supplying resources
explanation.paragraph: `pipelines/layouts.rs` combines those entries into the renderer's shared contracts. The line group supplies pen/view settings and clipping planes. The object group supplies row data and relative translations. The ink variant additionally declares single-sample and multisampled depth/identity textures, projected triangles and tile lists. A shader's group and binding numbers must match this contract; reordering a Rust array without preserving its explicit binding numbers changes which resource a shader reads.

explanation.heading: ### Placement and bounds
explanation.paragraph: `hull.rs`, `instance.rs`, `objects.rs` and `pipelines/mod.rs` expose narrow module interfaces. The rows checkpoint re-exports hull geometry, the instance layout, the object table and pipeline layouts/cache. Rendering later registers hull upload, GPU validation, ink/lane code and vertex-layout construction through these same indices. A `pub use` makes an existing type available to a caller; it neither duplicates that type nor creates another buffer owner.

explanation.heading: ### Validate a replacement before changing the document
explanation.paragraph: For a changed set, a map of prior runs by ID lets unchanged layout reuse its shaped buffer. Moving or recoloring a label does not require reshaping its glyph sequence. Changing text or metrics does. Replacing fonts validates the new sources and reshapes against the new font system, advancing both font and document revisions. Cache reuse follows the inputs that determine layout, not whether a label happened to be drawn last frame.

explanation.heading: ### Choose an assertion that detects the rendering defect
explanation.paragraph: Font coverage tests enumerate command names, aliases, options and hints against the bundled subsets, then check representative accented text and UI symbols. A specimen intentionally outside the subset is shaped after replacing the fonts with the complete font files, and every resulting glyph ID must be nonzero. This proves local character coverage and replacement behavior; it does not exercise asynchronous browser font delivery or compare glyph edge quality.

explanation.heading: ## Prerequisites and ownership
explanation.paragraph: The crate root `lib.rs` declares the top-level modules. Its `shader!` macro expands to a compile-time include from the build output directory when a later shader uses it; declaring a macro does not compile a render pipeline. The tutorial entry is enabled only for wasm with the tutorial feature. The eventual native self-test and production web entry have different target gates, so a browser-only item is not accidentally required by a native build.

explanation.heading: ### Separate CPU construction from GPU rendering
explanation.paragraph: `selftest::render_scene` loads actual documents, creates a headless `Gpu`, frames the scene, settles display refinement and renders offscreen. Its environment controls select a camera, viewport, clipping, labels or repeated orbit frames. Record those controls with the result. Refinement is bounded by row count and fails if it cannot settle; capturing an unfinished frame would conflate refinement with a rendering regression.

explanation.heading: ### Use an independent question as an oracle
explanation.paragraph: `selftest::lifecycle` compares color and object/subobject ID images through resize, rewalk, edits/undo and reload. Each nonzero ID must still resolve to scene identity. Matching color alone could hide a broken selection map; matching IDs alone could hide a rendering defect.

explanation.heading: ### Use an independent question as an oracle
explanation.paragraph: `selftest::oracle` asks a CPU ray-visibility question for samples along strokes against placed triangles. It compares clearly visible samples with nearby rendered ink. Its clearance avoids deciding ambiguous coplanar cases using the GPU's own tolerance. This checks hidden-line visibility without merely repeating the shader's output as the expected answer.

explanation.heading: ### Separate CPU construction from GPU rendering
explanation.paragraph: `selftest::profile` times the geometry walk by object kind before GPU drawing. Its BRep measurements separate meshing, edge chains and orientation work. A slow walk suggests different work from a slow draw; reducing shader complexity cannot remove time spent constructing triangles on the CPU.

explanation.heading: ### Use an independent question as an oracle
explanation.paragraph: `selftest::stroke_witness` exposes controlled rendering inputs and returns pixels, identity, shader sources and device/queue ownership. The sheet witness explicitly requires a verified software adapter. The renderer's cloud witness serves the corresponding cloud checks. A software witness is reproducible pipeline evidence; it does not demonstrate a hardware driver's behavior or a phone's speed.

explanation.heading: ### Reconstruct ambient shading from visible geometry
explanation.paragraph: `ambient_composite.wgsl` overlays black with the computed occlusion as alpha. Its multisample edge path draws only listed sixteen-pixel tiles and unpacks one correction byte per sample. The output sample mask selects the corrected sample instead of darkening every sample in a partly covered pixel. This separates smooth interior shading from edge coverage and preserves the attachment's multisample identity.

explanation.heading: ### Reconstruct ambient shading from visible geometry
explanation.paragraph: `ambient_depth.wgsl` builds coarser depth levels by selecting the nearest positive linear depth from each two-by-two block and carrying that sample's radius with it. Empty blocks retain zero depth. Its occupancy pass searches a five-by-five neighbourhood for any geometry, expanding the active region enough for nearby sampling. Reducing depth and radius together prevents a coarse sample from combining one surface's location with another object's shading scale.

explanation.heading: ### Reconstruct ambient shading from visible geometry
explanation.paragraph: `ambient_geometry.wgsl` resolves the physical primitive ID through the instance slot table before reading triangle vertices and their placed owner. It derives a normal from transformed triangle edges, avoiding dependence on a possibly smoothed vertex normal. Pixels without a triangle reconstruct a normal from depth neighbours, choosing nearby samples to avoid crossing a discontinuity. The normal is then oriented toward the camera. This geometry lookup lets identical definition triangles shade differently under distinct instance transforms.

explanation.heading: ### The arrow function boundary
explanation.paragraph: The shared `arrow_corner` shader receives individual fields. An observed Android driver failure changed `end` and `heads` when a packed row structure crossed that function boundary. Keeping the arguments separate is a compatibility requirement; passing a convenient `VectorRow` value would reintroduce the failing interface.

explanation.heading: ### Pass order and visibility
explanation.paragraph: `background.wgsl` generates one oversized triangle from three vertex indices, covering the viewport without a diagonal between two triangles. Its fragment output is white, or slightly grey when ambient shading is active, and writes zero primitive identity. The backdrop therefore contributes visible color but cannot masquerade as an object triangle in subsequent visibility queries.

explanation.heading: ### A section cap needs depth and identity too
explanation.paragraph: `cap.wgsl` draws the section's hatch/color, writes the plane's depth and a cap primitive marker, and supplies the covered sample mask. Other clipping planes still constrain that mask. Caps therefore participate in visibility and selection rather than being a flat color pasted over the final frame. Plane origin and hatch direction keep hatch coordinates tied to the authored section.

explanation.heading: ### Shared shader records and coordinate rules
explanation.paragraph: `clip.wgsl` declares six world and screen clipping planes, hatch transforms and sample settings. A clipping-plane object is exempt from its own cutting test. Surface distance subtracts a scale-aware slack so a coplanar face yields consistently to its section cap; ink uses a separate dot-product rounding allowance to avoid dropping a line on the plane. `CLIPPING` can specialize unused tests away. This is the common data and predicate contract; the later visibility chapter connects it to crossing counts, cap rendering and sampled depth.

explanation.heading: ### Compare ink with the right surface
explanation.paragraph: `face_coverage.wgsl` derives surface coverage from nonzero primitive IDs at each sample. One entry returns the fraction of covered samples; another writes full coverage only to the corresponding sample mask. Empty pixels discard. These are different outputs for different downstream passes: an averaged coverage value cannot replace an exact per-sample mask at a multisampled edge.

explanation.heading: ### Draw dots and vertex markers
explanation.paragraph: `glyph.wgsl` projects each dot centre and expands a triangle around its disc in screen space. Negative radii stay in pixels; positive radii are projected from scene units. Very small discs retain a half-pixel footprint and fade instead of flickering away. The fragment stage computes circular coverage before expensive visibility reads. Picking requires sufficient coverage and rejects non-pickable object rows; ordinary dots encode a marker tag, while source-query dots use the supplied point row. A visible dot and its pick identity therefore share placement but need different output encodings.

explanation.heading: ### Pass order and visibility
explanation.paragraph: `grid.wgsl` generates eleven lines in each construction-plane direction at 1,000-unit spacing, extending 5,000 units either side of the origin, plus three colored axes. The vertex index determines the line and endpoint; no grid vertex buffer is needed. Each local point is expanded through the supplied frame axes and origin before camera projection. This construction grid is separate from a selectable plane object and writes no primitive identity.

explanation.heading: ### Compare ink with the right surface
explanation.paragraph: `triangle.wgsl` writes surface color, depth and primitive identity. `ink_visibility.wgsl` consumes the single-sample or multisampled versions of those attachments and the tile lists. It accounts for local depth slope and the geometric sag between a curved edge and its faceted surface; a fixed global depth offset would either hide legitimate edges or expose strokes through unrelated geometry.

explanation.heading: ### Kernel Matrix display
explanation.paragraph: `matrix.wgsl` expands the quad in cell coordinates, with cell zero centred on the object origin and later rows extending downward. The fragment stage finds the cell and reads its packed value. Numeric labels are generated from seven-segment digits, a minus sign and decimal point; trailing decimal zeros are dropped. They are not glyph-atlas text, so this small numeric display does not load a font. The header supplies zero/minimum/maximum colors and the nonzero range, allowing zero cells to remain visually distinct.

explanation.heading: ### Shared shader records and coordinate rules
explanation.paragraph: `normals.wgsl` uses cofactors to apply the inverse-transpose direction transform. A normal cannot be transformed like a point under nonuniform scale. The determinant sign preserves orientation under reflection; a degenerate matrix or zero input normal yields zero instead of normalizing an invalid vector. Octahedral decoding unfolds two packed components into a unit direction; the 32-bit path reserves `0x80008000` for an absent normal. That sentinel must remain distinct from an ordinary direction.

explanation.heading: ### Shared shader records and coordinate rules
explanation.paragraph: `physical.wgsl` separates colour output from object/subobject identity and carries a triangle identity alongside both. Triangle IDs are split into low and high 16-bit halves because the selected four-sample target format cannot store the required 32-bit channel directly. Zero represents no triangle; callers use a nonzero encoded identity for geometry. This storage choice must agree between writing a fragment and interpreting a visibility sample.

explanation.heading: ### Generate planes and arrows from compact rows
explanation.paragraph: `plane.wgsl` derives each grid endpoint from the vertex index and the stored frame. Eleven positions along each axis produce the ten-by-ten grid. The z direction is the cross product of x and y. Grid segments call the shared arrow function without heads and with ordinary depth behavior; the three colored axis arrows request end heads and the overlay variant. This explains why a solid can hide the grey grid while the orientation arrows remain readable.

explanation.heading: ### Project once, then restrict each visibility query
explanation.paragraph: `project_triangles.wgsl` transforms triangles into screen-space records described by `projected_triangle.wgsl`. Each record carries clipped coverage, edge equations, bounds and depth information. `triangle_tiles.rs` manages those buffers and binds the current geometry, object transforms and slot table. If an allocation moves, it rebuilds the binding that holds the old handle.

explanation.heading: ### Shared shader records and coordinate rules
explanation.paragraph: `projected_triangle.wgsl` stores edge equations, a depth reference and gradient, screen bounds and a corner count in a 96-byte record. A clipped triangle may have four corners. Coverage first rejects empty records and points outside the bounds, then checks signed edge distances with a 1/256-pixel allowance for rasterizer snapping. Depth comes from the reference plus the gradient at that pixel. Tile span doubles until the canvas uses at most 262,144 tiles; the Rust tile layout must make the same choice.

explanation.heading: ### Strokes, dashes and reveal
explanation.paragraph: `ribbon.wgsl` builds each six-vertex stroke quad in screen space, with widths projected independently at its endpoints. Neighbour cut planes join a chain without double coverage; marker trims and arrowhead cut planes remove covered shaft ends. Dash coverage includes the stored cumulative offset, while reveal moves each segment endpoint toward its own start. Silhouette-only segments inspect the sag sign bit and adjacent face orientation. Fragment coverage is evaluated before the shared visibility query; the color and mask passes use the same centre-line clipping and surface test.

explanation.heading: ### Project once, then restrict each visibility query
explanation.paragraph: The exclusive prefix sum gives each tile the sum of earlier counts, which becomes its list offset. Workgroup memory lets 256 invocations cooperate; barriers ensure that one iteration reads a completed prior iteration. Further scan passes combine block totals and add those offsets to each tile. Counts saturate at capacity instead of wrapping into apparently valid small offsets.

explanation.heading: ### Shared shader records and coordinate rules
explanation.paragraph: `scene.wgsl` declares the shader side of the same contract: the camera matrix in group zero, line/clipping uniforms in group one, and object rows plus separate translations in group two. Its `Instance` is 112 bytes and its `LineUniform` is 80 bytes. `place` applies the row's model matrix before adding the scene-relative translation. The non-pickable flag is independent of colour and visibility; selected colour, layer colour and edge colour have separate rules. Field order and padding must agree with the Rust uploads, not merely have similarly spelled names.

explanation.heading: ### Keep allocation, identity and frame state separate
explanation.paragraph: `placed_triangle` reverses a one-based visible triangle ID into an arena triangle and an optional instance-row override. The slot texture is 1,024 texels wide; its header gives the instance count and ordinary arena range. Ordinary IDs keep `SLOT_OWN_ROW`. For an instance ID, binary search finds the last slot whose ID range starts before it, then a range check rejects gaps. This makes a picked or shaded instance refer to its own placement while reusing the definition triangle. Zero and out-of-range IDs return `NO_TRIANGLE`.

explanation.heading: ### Draw dots and vertex markers
explanation.paragraph: `sphere.wgsl` uses the marker template and neighbouring face normals to distinguish front-facing and back-facing vertex markers. Packed normals are transformed with the object before comparison to the eye direction. Markers shrink when projected vertex spacing is less than three diameters, with a minimum taper factor of 0.15, preventing a dense mesh from becoming a solid field of dots. Its color and ID entry points share coverage geometry; displaying a faint marker through translucent faces does not mean that an occluded marker is freely pickable.

explanation.heading: ### Render resident cloud points
explanation.paragraph: `gpu/splat.rs` turns selected ranges into bounded draw records. A record carries the combined camera/object matrix, point and normal offsets, radius information, tint, owner row and selected point. Its 160-byte Rust layout matches the shader's 40-word stride. Cumulative point counts let `splat.wgsl` locate a record by binary search when a single draw spans several runs. Six generated vertices form each point's quad; the shader computes its actual coverage and depth.

explanation.heading: ### Render resident cloud points
explanation.paragraph: `splat_resolve.wgsl` copies valid point color and reverse-Z depth into the scene. Empty point pixels have zero depth and are discarded. Optional eye-dome lighting compares neighboring logarithmic depths to darken depth boundaries. The ID pass instead writes the object row and point row, so picking and visible color have distinct outputs while using the same point coverage. Original source IDs are resolved by the later source-query adapter; a temporary GPU row is not that persistent identity.

explanation.heading: ### Reconstruct ambient shading from visible geometry
explanation.paragraph: `ssao.wgsl` estimates screen-space occlusion by sampling horizons in several directions around the reconstructed surface point. Sample distance grows quadratically and selects coarser depth levels farther away. Object radius, bias and a finite screen radius bound the effect. Two directional filters use depth/normal agreement to avoid blurring across unrelated surfaces. Reprojected history is accepted only when its signed depth agrees, then clamped to the current neighbourhood before blending. This is an approximation using visible depth; it cannot infer arbitrary hidden geometry.

explanation.heading: ### Shade and outline the resulting surface coverage
explanation.paragraph: `surface_outline.rs` renders coverage masks, resolves multisampled coverage when needed, and builds coarse and dilated masks to skip empty regions. `face_coverage.wgsl` produces coverage; `surface_outline.wgsl` composites the border using a bounded offset table. Selection outlines and ordinary borders can then use the appropriate masks without confusing object IDs with coverage values.

explanation.heading: ### Text resources
explanation.paragraph: `text_outline.wgsl` renders triangulated text through the arena instead of sampling a glyph texture. The vertex stage applies object placement, tint, selection and hidden state. The fragment stage clips in canvas coordinates and outputs flat color. Its physical-ID output carries the owning object but no surface-triangle identity; text therefore remains selectable without becoming a solid face for geometric visibility reconstruction.

explanation.heading: ### Text resources
explanation.paragraph: `text_plane.wgsl` samples rasterized glyph coverage on vertices already projected from an authored world plane. A screen clip box cuts the label; a rounded plate can supply black or selected-yellow background. The shader evaluates derivative-dependent coverage uniformly before choosing bare glyphs or a plate. Picking uses the same transformed label footprint and object identity. The pick shape is the rounded label area, not a per-glyph alpha test, so spaces within a label can still select it.

explanation.heading: ### Text resources
explanation.paragraph: `text_plate.wgsl` computes signed distance to the original rounded rectangle and uses screen derivatives to soften its edge. Selection changes the black plate to yellow. The ID entry applies the pick-window transform and rejects pixels outside the rounded boundary or without an object. It writes the already encoded object-row-plus-one value, keeping an empty pixel distinct from row zero.

explanation.heading: ### Compare ink with the right surface
explanation.paragraph: `triangle.wgsl` shares transformed vertices across face color, source-face picking, selection masks and clipping counts. Mirrored object transforms reverse the interpretation of raster front-facing state. A supplied normal is normalized; missing normals fall back to screen derivatives. Closed translucent solids drop back faces and use the global opacity, while open or printed surfaces follow their own rules. Color writes also carry primitive identity; clipped color uses a per-sample kept-side mask. Keeping these outputs together makes visible surfaces, selected faces and ink occlusion agree on the same placed geometry.

explanation.heading: ### Project once, then restrict each visibility query
explanation.paragraph: The screen is divided into tiles. Tile width grows when necessary to bound total tile count. `triangle_tiles.wgsl` draws a four-corner rectangle over the tiles touched by a triangle's bounds, then rejects tiles outside its edge equations. This uses rasterization to find relevant tiles rather than testing every triangle for every ink pixel.

explanation.heading: ### Generate planes and arrows from compact rows
explanation.paragraph: `vector.wgsl` is the thin entry adapter for the shared arrow implementation. The instance index selects a stored vector row and the vertex index selects one of eighteen generated corners. It passes every endpoint, pen, head and trim field individually to `arrow_corner`, with the ordinary depth variant. Keep this field-by-field call when adding another arrow producer; the driver constraint described above applies at the shared function boundary, even when the caller already has a convenient packed row.

explanation.heading: ### Keep the manipulation widget independent of scene depth
explanation.paragraph: `widget.wgsl` transforms mesh vertices into the tile and changes the active handle to orange. A second vertex entry maps a six-vertex quad into the tile's canvas rectangle. The composite fragment divides sampled RGB by alpha, guarded against zero, before returning color and alpha for blending. The widget therefore has its own small rendering/compositing contract rather than borrowing the scene-object shader and its selection rules.

explanation.heading: ### One owner for changing state
explanation.paragraph: `State` owns the window handle, GPU, camera, loaded scene and selection. These objects need a common lifetime: a document upload changes both scene rows and GPU buffers, and a selection result changes both application state and its next image. `Arc<Window>` keeps the window alive while asynchronous setup and redraw callbacks retain handles to it; it does not make the scene a shared mutable object.

explanation.heading: ### Keep selection requests tied to their initiating gesture
explanation.paragraph: A box-selection gesture stores both corners in device pixels. Left-to-right means a window that contains whole objects; right-to-left means a crossing that touches them, drawn with a dashed outline. Starting is refused while drawing or splitting owns input. Release applies Ctrl removal before Shift addition and reports both matched and resulting selected counts. The overlay visualizes the pending region; selection changes only when the gesture finishes.

explanation.heading: ### Change drawing and viewing context
explanation.paragraph: `state/clipping.rs` gathers each clipping plane from its current GPU row placement, so preview dragging moves the cut immediately. Hiding its rectangle does not disable its cut; the host reports that distinction when a plane becomes hidden. The first active cut verifies previously walked mesh solid orientation, sharing the result for instances of one geometry. Creation enforces the maximum plane count and uses document history, whereas On/Off and fill change rendering state. Flipping replaces the selected plane geometry and synchronizes its rows.

explanation.heading: ### Keep selection requests tied to their initiating gesture
explanation.paragraph: The cloud-query state adapter starts only in streamed-cloud control mode and assigns each request a generation. It combines camera projection with cloud placement and converts the CSS selection aperture into device pixels. Source pages produce temporary GPU-pick candidates while displayed LOD remains bounded; after eligible pages are checked, the winner is resolved to its original source ID. View or selection changes cancel the query. Batches with another generation or a cancelled token cannot replace the current selection.

explanation.heading: ### A delayed pick still belongs to the original drag
explanation.paragraph: `ObjectDrag` retains the press, latest cursor and whether release arrived before the GPU answer. A late hit after release applies the accumulated move; a miss becomes rectangle selection. While held, a hit starts following and a miss starts the selection rectangle. Retaining the release state prevents a quick flick from disappearing merely because readback took another frame.

explanation.heading: ### A draft owns incomplete input
explanation.paragraph: `state/drawing.rs::Draft` holds accepted points, hover position, plane, construction kind and an optional tool. Fixed-point constructions finish when their required point count is reached; open constructions finish through their explicit completion action. Rectangle and polygon constructions derive geometry in the chosen plane, so their preview and final points share a frame.

explanation.heading: ### Keep fast previews subordinate to the document
explanation.paragraph: A gizmo drag retains original placements, the selected subobject target and source geometry. Its center comes from the selection bounds or the selected controls transformed into world space. Pointer motion previews; release first restores original display placements, then commits the final delta through whole-object or subobject editing. A rejected subobject edit restores source rendering. Cancellation restores cached GPU geometry or rewalks the source, restores group placements and clears the gesture. A click without a drag opens the numeric handle input instead of creating an edit.

explanation.heading: ### Register state and frame responsibilities
explanation.paragraph: `Features` owns optional interaction state across frames: drafts, active drags, pending splits, query generations, snapping and hierarchy state. Ordered function lists declare work before and after pick answers, handlers that may consume a pick before ordinary selection, and hooks that expand a clicked row into a group. A feature registers its state and hooks at these boundaries instead of rewriting the event loop. Order is behavior: a pending drag must receive its delayed answer before ordinary selection interprets it.

explanation.heading: ### Restore editable geometry only when needed
explanation.paragraph: A display can retain rows after releasing its kernel geometry. `locked_reason` distinguishes a permanently read-only streamed shell from a released document whose source can be fetched again. Requested operations enter a small `Resume` queue. The returned `Hydrated` value carries a document index and token; an old token is ignored after replacement or another release.

explanation.heading: ### Keep numeric input attached to its handle
explanation.paragraph: The numeric-input state adapter projects the active gizmo handle to CSS coordinates and supplies its title, units and neutral-value hint. Parsing an empty or neutral value can close the box without changing geometry. A valid value becomes the handle transform and uses the common apply operation with a move, rotate or scale history label. Invalid parsing keeps the prompt available for correction; an apply failure reports status after closure. A tap that opens the box requests the phone keyboard through feedback.

explanation.heading: ### Resolve panel colour actions by identity
explanation.paragraph: Panel colour actions decode the node key and distinguish face from edge channels. They resolve the document and GUID before changing the corresponding override map; choosing the original colour removes an override. Edge colour is only applicable to a row with faces. The adapter updates GPU presentation and refreshes application state after the scene change. A panel row number alone is insufficient: the stored override must remain attached to the same document object across hierarchy rebuilding.

explanation.heading: ### Keep selection requests tied to their initiating gesture
explanation.paragraph: Picking a sheet entity highlights its edge within the parent row rather than selecting the whole sheet; picking the same entity again clears selection. A new generation identifies its optional metadata request. Matching responses cache the side table and expose the entity name and kind; stale or cancelled responses are ignored. A missing metadata URL still permits selection by entity ID, while a metadata error is reported without inventing a name.

explanation.heading: ### Keep a pending split until it can run
explanation.paragraph: The split state retains the target, optional face and chosen cutters. Confirming without a cutter restores the pending state and asks for one instead of losing the selection. Before running the scene operation it removes temporary cutter highlighting. A successful division refreshes history and finds the target again by document/GUID after synchronization; the BRep remains joined and cutters remain present. A no-division result or error restores the gizmo. These transitions make Enter, panel clicks and pointer selection share one pending operation.

explanation.heading: ### A document title is an object
explanation.paragraph: `state/text.rs::annotate_document` measures newly added BRep and surface bounds and places a nameplate above them. `scene_text.rs` registers it as a text row with its own identity. Hiding document geometry and deleting all selected rows therefore have different effects: hide can leave the title visible, while Delete removes the separately selected title too. Undo restores the joined transaction.

explanation.heading: ### Continue a tool without borrowing its host twice
explanation.paragraph: `state/tool.rs` saves original row placements for previews. Cursor motion applies temporary placements; accepting input uses the normal edit transaction. Cancelling restores those placements and keeps selection. Thus ten preview moves followed by Escape do not create ten undo entries. `choices.rs` and `options.rs` provide option selection through the same tool contract, including command-line buttons for touch input.

explanation.heading: ### A document title is an object
explanation.paragraph: The `text_quality.rs` diagnostic page compares the actual text lane with browser text at several sizes, including accents, combining characters and fallback symbols. It owns its own test surface and calls the production lane. This is a diagnostic fixture, not a replacement production text implementation or proof that every device renders the same glyph edges.
